projects.problem: Lipid nanoparticle design involves selecting lipid identities and mixing ratios within a constrained search space. This project explored how to discover promising formulations under a limited model-evaluation budget.
projects.approach:
I led the design and implementation of a constrained black-box optimizer, using the pretrained COMET model to score candidate formulations. The search combined Qiskit circuits and SPSA optimization across 6,048 feasible combinations of lipid identities and mixing ratios.

I benchmarked candidate discovery against random search using matched evaluation budgets.
projects.outcome: Winner of the IBM Quantum Qiskit Fall Fest Hackathon. In one simulation run, the mean sampled COMET score increased from -3.06 to 5.16.

caseStudies.title: Multimodal Retrieval & RAG Evaluation
caseStudies.description: Building multimodal retrieval and tracing evidence loss in a product question-answering system.

content.text: Multimodal Retrieval & RAG Evaluation
KAIST Auto-ID Labs · AI Research Engineer Intern · May–August 2026

At KAIST Auto-ID Labs, our team built a system that lets people scan a product and ask questions about it. A GS1 Digital Link identifies the product and leads to its resources, such as a care label, a product page or a storage video.
I built the multimodal retrieval layer and later developed the dataset and evaluation tools we used to investigate failures.
Vector Search

I made label photos searchable by describing their contents in text. For video, I combined speech transcripts and frame descriptions into timestamped passages, embedded each passage and ranked it against the question. When I asked in Korean how to store a sweater, 00:44–00:58 ranked first among the passages from a 57.6-second clothing-care video. The narrator recommends folding sweaters. Using that spoken evidence, the system answered in Korean that folding keeps the shoulders from stretching.
Parallel preprocessing
I ran speech transcription alongside visual analysis and requested captions for up to four video frames at a time. The chart compares this with sequential preprocessing on the same storage video.

One 57.6-second video, one run per configuration using live APIs. Both configurations used eight scene-detected frames sampled across the video; parallel processing allowed up to four caption requests at once. These times cover preprocessing only; indexing, search and answer synthesis were measured separately.
Frame sampling

Selecting the first eight of 17 detected scenes left the last representative frame at 19.5 seconds. I changed the selection to sample eight frames evenly across the detected scenes, extending coverage to 54.5 seconds, and added a regression test. This fixed missing visual information near the end of the video. The sweater answer above came from speech, not from the selected frame.
Proposed Design: resource queue + autorater

attrs.alt: The proposed external retrieval queue checks incoming evidence before generating an answer. A final critic reviews the answer.

content.text: Design proposal from the internship presentation.

I also investigated when the system had enough evidence to answer. If the care label already gives the washing temperature, should the user have to wait for a storage video? I proposed keeping the knowledge graph as the first lookup. When external retrieval is needed, completed items enter a resource queue. An autorater checks whether the accumulated evidence supports an answer to the question. Once it does, the system can generate the answer and pass it to the final critic.

The autorater checks the question and evidence before generation; the final critic also reviews the generated answer. At the time, we had no suitable benchmark for testing that decision. The later benchmark evaluated the existing pipeline. The proposed gate’s latency and its risk of stopping before essential evidence arrives remain unmeasured.
A follow-up experiment would compare waiting for all resources against the queue on the same questions, measuring both latency and the rate of missing essential evidence.
Benchmark

In a June test, the question was which brand made a T-shirt. The graph returned the product and its care instructions. The brand was missing, yet the first critic ended the search before the system opened an external source. Seeing only the final answer would hide that routing decision.

I built a benchmark that records both the expected answer and where to find it. I extracted facts from public records, preserved the original field for each value, and used the facts to generate linked pages and reference answers. For Barilla pesto, Open Food Facts gives
22.3 g of fat per serving
. I also generated a nutrition page showing
so we could test whether the answer would change with the source.

In July I evaluated the existing pipeline on 20 foods and attractions. I started the run at external retrieval, skipping the graph lookup and first critic, and used the original pages and a warm cache. Of
216 single-hop questions, 179 earned full credit (82.9%)
. Another 20 earned partial credit, 12 went unanswered, and five drew incorrect answers. In both cases below, the system said it couldn’t confirm the answer.
Question
What the trace showed
Where it failed
How tall is Busan Tower?
The system opened the right page. Its body said
, but the extractor kept only a structured metadata block containing the tower’s name. The answer model never saw the height.
Page extraction
What is Gamcheon Culture Village’s nickname?
“Korea’s Machu Picchu”
reached the answer model. Its response cited a sculpture from an image description and said it could not confirm the nickname.
Answer generation

Of the 37 cases that missed full credit, I traced six to source selection, six to page extraction and nine to answer generation. Eight exposed packaging facts I had placed on storage-instruction pages. In the remaining eight, I flagged the grader for potentially penalizing correct answers that included extra detail.
The benchmark also had a blind spot. All
11 image questions

earned full credit. Every answer cited the HTML nutrition table, and only two also cited the label photo. To measure whether the system can read a label, I would repeat those questions with the duplicate HTML evidence withheld. The July run contained no video questions.
By the August handover, the merged corpus covered
100,831 records
across food products, tourist attractions and drug labels. Each of its
retained a reference to the source field a reviewer could use to check it.

caseStudies.title: LipoQ
caseStudies.description: Quantum-assisted search over 6,048 lipid nanoparticle formulations, evaluated with a fixed COMET model and compared with random search under the same distinct-candidate budget.

content.text: LipoQ
Quantum-assisted search for lipid nanoparticle formulations
Winner — Qiskit Fall Fest Hackathon 2026, University of Waterloo
2 days · Lead developer · Python · Qiskit · PyTorch · SciPy

Designing a lipid nanoparticle formulation involves choosing both the lipid ingredients and their proportions. LipoQ explores whether a trainable quantum circuit can learn to generate candidates with higher predicted scores. I led development and wrote most of the code over two days, building a working pipeline from candidate generation to evaluation and comparison.
Quantum-assisted search
The search covers
6,048 possible formulations
, combining 84 lipid combinations with 72 valid ratio settings. A
14-qubit circuit
samples candidates, and a decoder maps each measurement to a formulation that satisfies the composition constraints, including proportions that sum to one.
Each candidate is evaluated by
COMET

, an existing pretrained model for lipid nanoparticle design. COMET stays fixed throughout the experiment. A classical optimizer, SPSA, uses its predictions to update the circuit parameters and guide the next round of sampling.

attrs.alt: LipoQ pipeline: a trainable 14-qubit circuit samples constrained lipid formulations, the frozen COMET model predicts their scores, and SPSA updates the circuit. Random search provides an independent comparison with the same distinct-candidate budget.

content.text: Quantum sampling, COMET evaluation, and classical feedback.
Evaluation

To assess the search, I added a random-search baseline with the same number of distinct candidates. Prediction caching avoids repeated model inference, while saved configurations, candidate records, and automatic plots make each run easier to inspect and reproduce. Both methods use shared evaluation and reporting code to keep the comparison consistent.
In one local simulator run, the circuit's sampled mean COMET score rose from
. After evaluating
4,682 distinct formulations per method
, both quantum and random search reached the same best score of
. The sampled scores improved during training, but the best candidate did not outperform the baseline. These results describe model predictions; biological performance was not tested.

caseStudies.title: Qubit Reuse and Mapping in Distributed Quantum Computing
caseStudies.description: Comparing two qubit-reuse plans for a six-qubit circuit on two processors: four physical qubits in both plans, but one transfer versus none.

content.text: Qubit Reuse and Mapping in Distributed Quantum Computing
Capstone research · In progress · Sep 2026 — Present

I tested a circuit designed for six qubits on a model with two quantum processors. Each processor had two physical qubits. After measurement and reset, a qubit can be used again. This allowed the circuit to fit into the four available places.

I compared two reuse plans. Both used four physical qubits and had nine layers of operations before communication steps were added. This comparison is a motivational example for the project: minimizing the number of qubits does not necessarily minimize communication between processors.
How qubit reuse changes communication
The first plan needs one transfer

attrs.alt: QARMA-R-based reuse plan on two processors, each with two physical qubits. The red line marks the required transfer between processors.

content.text: A rule based on QARMA-R chose to reuse q₂ for q₄ and q₃ for q₅. I checked all allowed ways to place and move the qubits. Even the best arrangement needed one transfer between processors. The red line in the first image shows that transfer.
The second plan needs no transfers

attrs.alt: Alternative reuse plan: q₂ is reused for q₅ and q₃ for q₄, keeping each interacting pair on the same processor without a transfer.

content.text: I changed the pairs so that q₂ was reused for q₅ and q₃ for q₄. This kept q₅ with q₀, and q₄ with q₁, on the same processor. Each pair could then work together without a transfer.

The reuse rule saved qubits, yet another plan needed fewer transfers. This is the counterexample I found. During the search, each plan kept the same order and grouping of operations. Qiskit Aer simulations also confirmed that both plans kept the original measurement probabilities, within rounding error.
An earlier test used a simpler model and 60 generated circuits. It found nine similar cases, even when moving a freshly reset qubit between processors was free.

caseStudies.title: The Pet Mischief Detector
caseStudies.description: A team project combining object detection and relative depth to flag potentially risky interactions between pets and household objects.

content.text: The Pet Mischief Detector
Computer vision · Team project · Apr 2026
A prototype that looks at photos and flags interactions where a pet could knock over or break a household object.
Python · PyTorch · YOLO · Depth Anything V2 · OpenCV
Detection & Depth

Moving the camera changes how far apart objects appear, even when the objects stay in place. I proposed adding relative depth to YOLO detections to help interpret these relationships. The team combined proximity, bounding-box overlap, and depth information to assign an attention level to each scene. The system covers eight classes, including cats, dogs, cups, and vases.
Photo → YOLO detection → Depth Anything V2 → relationship scores → LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH
A cat and a glass

attrs.alt: A cat with its head inside a glass. YOLO26s detects the cat and cup, and the system displays HIGH. A relative depth map appears in the lower right.

content.text: A cat with its head inside a glass, marked HIGH by the system. This contact could tip or break the glass; no breakage is visible. Team-project output · COCO image 469317 · YOLO26s.
Contribution & Evaluation

I identified the limits of judging distance from 2D positions and proposed adding depth estimation. I ran and checked the full process, from detection and depth estimation to scoring and visual output.
I wrote the image-level risk evaluation script and compared model predictions and confusion matrices. A teammate implemented the main pipeline and updated the scoring rules.
Checking class labels before scoring

The pretrained YOLO model used class index 15 for “cat,” while our eight-class dataset used 0. Comparing those numbers directly treated the same object as different classes. I used an inference path that selected objects by class name, then built an evaluation process that compared each image’s predicted risk level with its label. Checking what the class numbers meant was an essential step before evaluating the results.
Interpreting the attention level
The attention levels come from rules about spatial relationships. They do not measure accident probability or physical distance.
